name: libmps
why: Ravenbrook's Memory Pool System, an unusual memory management framework worth reading about even if the library is obscure.

brief.what_it_is: The Memory Pool System (MPS) is a C memory management library from Ravenbrook Limited, distributed as the MPS Kit: source code, manuals, and design documentation. You compile mps.c into an object file and link it into your own program, which then asks the MPS for memory through its allocation interfaces. It ships with a library of memory pool classes, each implementing a different memory management policy. The brew package is named libmps and installs no executables, so it is a library for developers, not a command-line tool.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the MPS exists to be a very general, adaptable, flexible, reliable, and efficient memory management system that lets you combine memory management techniques flexibly. It is meant to support both manual and automatic memory management in one framework. The project has been in development since 1994 and in commercial products since 1997.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals. It lists the features the MPS supports: in-line allocation, finalization, weakness, and multiple concurrent cooperating incremental generational garbage collections. Its pool classes provide specialized policies, and the design details live in the manual and design documents that the README points to.

commands_seen.context: Change into the code directory of the MPS Kit before compiling the library.
Unix or macOS build (with the Xcode command line tools): compiles mps.c into an object file to link into your project.
Windows build (with the Microsoft SDK or Visual Studio 2010): the same compile step using the MSVC compiler.

brief.install_notes: There is no brew binary. The MPS Kit is distributed as source and must be built before use. The basic build is a single compile of mps.c, with the command shown in commands_seen. For configuration, building the manual, the libraries and tests, IDE use, and autoconf, the README sends you to the build guide at manual/build.txt. The Scheme interpreter in the example/scheme directory is the README's worked example of using the MPS. Supported platforms are Windows Vista or later (IA-32 and x86-64, Microsoft Visual C/C++), Linux 2.6 or later (IA-32 with GCC, x86-64 with GCC or Clang/LLVM), FreeBSD 7 or later (IA-32 and x86-64, GCC or Clang/LLVM), and macOS 10.4 or later (x86-64, Clang/LLVM). Reading the manual is described as essential before programming against the MPS.
brief.standout: It is a garbage collection and memory management framework rather than a single allocator. You choose and combine manual and automatic policies, including incremental generational collection, through its pool classes. It has been in commercial use since 1997, and the README claims that bugs are almost unknown in production.
brief.status: Likely maintained, but not verified. The README says the MPS is under continuous development and support by Ravenbrook. Its revision history runs to 2023-02-02, when the project migrated from Ravenbrook's Perforce to GitHub. The README's header is dated 2002, and the most recent licence change is 2020. I did not check commit dates or release tags.
brief.caveats: The Ravenbrook homepage returned HTTP 503, so this brief rests on the repository's readme.txt. The MPS is source-only and needs a build step; no binaries are provided. The supported platforms are narrow: no ARM or Apple Silicon is listed, and macOS support is x86-64 only. A 32-bit multi-threaded application on 64-bit Windows 7 under WOW64 needs a Microsoft hotfix, per the README. The licence is BSD 2-clause. The README's 'bugs are almost unknown' is the authors' own claim. Commercial support is available from Ravenbrook Limited.
quotes: The Memory Pool System (MPS) is a very general, adaptable, flexible, reliable, and efficient memory management system.
The MPS has been in development since 1994 and deployed in successful commercial products since 1997. Bugs are almost unknown in production.
The MPS Kit is distributed in source form. You need to build it before using it.

judge.reason: A little-known C framework for combining memory-management policies, including concurrent incremental generational garbage collection, offers a genuinely interesting idea to explore.

entry.title: libmps (Memory Pool System)
entry.tldr: A C memory management library, in development since 1994, that lets you mix manual allocation and incremental generational garbage collection through swappable pool classes.
entry.deeper_look:
The Memory Pool System (MPS) is a C library from Ravenbrook Limited. It ships as the MPS Kit: source, a manual, and design documentation. You compile one file, mps.c, into an object file and link it into your own program, which then requests memory through the MPS allocation interfaces. The brew package installs no executables, so this is a library for people writing runtimes, not a command-line tool.

The central idea is that memory management is a set of policies rather than one allocator. The MPS provides pool classes, each implementing a different policy, and you combine them within one program. Manual and automatic management live in the same framework. The README lists in-line allocation, finalization, weakness, and multiple concurrent cooperating incremental generational garbage collections.

The project was started in 1994 and has been in commercial products since 1997. In its own words: "Bugs are almost unknown in production." That is the authors' claim, not something verified here. It is old, and the age is part of the appeal: the design documents and manual record decades of thinking about how collectors and allocators fit together.

The README's worked example is a Scheme interpreter in the example/scheme directory. That is a good place to see what it looks like to build a language runtime on top of a collector you did not write. The README calls reading the manual essential before programming against the MPS.
entry.install:
brew install libmps
# Installs a library only, no executables. The MPS Kit is source-only and must be built: cd code, then compile mps.c. See manual/build.txt in the repository for configuration, tests and the manual. Needs a C compiler (Xcode command line tools on macOS).

try_this.what_happens: Moves into the code directory of the MPS Kit, where the library source lives.
Compiles the whole library into one object file (Unix or macOS) that you link into your own program.
The same single-file compile on Windows with the Microsoft compiler.

entry.whats_unique: It is a framework for memory management policies, not a single allocator or collector. You pick and combine manual and automatic pools, including incremental generational collection, in one program.
entry.caveats: Source-only with a build step, and the listed platforms are narrow (macOS x86-64 only, no ARM listed); the homepage returned 503 when checked, and the repository was not checked for recent commits.
